title: Test Accuracy vs. Generalization Gap: Model Selection in NLP without Accessing Training or Testing Data

problem.claim: Model selection requires metrics that can guide the choice of architecture and training hyperparameters without relying on test performance.

gap.claim: Prior empirical analyses of generalization metrics primarily focus on computer vision, generalization-gap prediction, and metrics that require data access.

contributions.claim: The paper evaluates generalization-metric-based model selection for NLP tasks, emphasizing metrics that directly predict test error and do not require access to data.

The analyses cover hundreds of Transformers trained under varied data amounts, model sizes, and optimization hyperparameters, 51 pretrained Transformers from eight Huggingface NLP model families, and 28 existing and novel generalization metrics.
The paper extends power-law spectral-distribution formulations to exponential and exponentially truncated power-law families.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe the work as providing the first model-selection results on large pretrained Huggingface Transformers using generalization metrics.

author_reported_evidence.claim: Metrics derived from the heavy-tail perspective exhibit stronger correlations with NLP task performance than other, more popular metrics.

narrative_sequence.summary: Model architecture and training hyperparameter selection is important for improving ML performance.
Recent studies use large-scale correlations in neural networks to identify generalization metrics for model selection, typically expecting correlation with test performance.
The study shifts the analysis toward NLP, direct test-error prediction, and metrics computable without data access.
The study evaluates diverse Transformer settings, Huggingface model families, and generalization metrics.
Heavy-tail-derived metrics are reported as particularly useful for NLP, and spectral formulations are extended to exponential and exponentially truncated power-law families.

source_observation.claim: Metrics derived from the heavy-tail perspective show stronger reported correlations than more popular metrics in the examined NLP tasks.

interpretation.claim: The usefulness of a generalization metric may depend on the task domain and the statistical perspective used to construct it.

application.claim: For NLP model selection, evaluate multiple metric families, including heavy-tail-derived metrics, rather than assuming metrics validated mainly in computer vision will transfer directly.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that heavy-tail-derived metrics outperform other metrics across all NLP tasks, model families, or training settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the NLP tasks, datasets, evaluation protocol, or exact correlation measures.
The abstract does not identify which metrics are data-free or provide their computational requirements.
The abstract does not report numerical correlation values or comparative statistical results.
The abstract does not provide implementation details or full-text evidence for the spectral-distribution extensions.
